summary: Specifies PNG, an extensible file format for lossless, portable, well-compressed storage of raster images. It was meant as a patent-free replacement for GIF. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: PNG is a way to save pictures so they stay sharp and compact. It was made as a free alternative to GIF.

questions: what is the difference between png and gif
subtitle: Lossless image format designed as a patent-free replacement for GIF.

tldr.problem: GIF was widely used for web images but was encumbered by patents on its compression algorithm, and lacked support for modern image types like truecolor and alpha transparency.
tldr.mechanism: PNG defines a file format with a flexible chunk-based structure that stores image data using the patent-free deflate/inflate compression, with support for multiple color modes, transparency, and metadata.
tldr.outcome: PNG became a widely adopted standard for lossless image compression on the web and in other applications, offering better compression than GIF and more features, though it is now Historic and superseded by other formats in some contexts.

today: RFC 2083 is Historic. PNG Version 1.0 remains widely used and implemented, particularly on the web and in scientific applications where lossless compression is essential. While newer formats have emerged for specialized purposes, PNG remains a stable, royalty-free standard that virtually all image software supports.

sections.title: What PNG Is
sections.content:
RFC 2083 specifies PNG (Portable Network Graphics), a lossless, well-compressed file format for raster images that runs on any platform without licensing restrictions. The initial goal was to replace GIF, which was patent-encumbered, but PNG proved valuable wherever images need to remain pixel-perfect after compression: web graphics, scientific data, and anywhere lossiness is unacceptable.

PNG was designed to be simple to implement, portable across operating systems, and robust against file corruption. It supports indexed color (up to 256 colors from a palette), grayscale, and truecolor (up to 16 bits per color channel), with optional per-pixel transparency via an alpha channel. Files can also include metadata like gamma correction and color space information to improve how they display on different screens.
sections.plainLanguage: PNG is a file format that keeps pictures exactly as they are, without throwing away details. It was invented so that everyone could use a good image format without needing permission from anyone.

sections.title: How PNG Files Are Built
sections.content:
Every PNG file starts with an 8-byte signature: the values 137, 80, 78, 71, 13, 10, 26, 10 (the bytes that would print as \x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n). This signature makes it easy to recognize a PNG file and detect common transmission errors early.

After the signature comes a series of chunks, each with a 4-byte length, a 4-byte type code, the chunk data, and a 4-byte CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) for error detection. Four critical chunks must appear in every valid PNG: IHDR (image header, always first), PLTE (palette, if needed), IDAT (the compressed image data itself, possibly split across multiple chunks), and IEND (the end marker, always last). Many optional ancillary chunks like gAMA (gamma), tEXt (text metadata), and tRNS (transparency) can appear between them.

The chunk layout is deliberately extensible: unknown chunks can be safely skipped or copied to a modified file, allowing PNG to evolve without breaking old decoders. Each chunk type's properties—whether it is critical or optional, whether it is safe to copy—are encoded directly in the ASCII letters of the chunk name.
sections.plainLanguage: A PNG file starts with a magic number that says 'I am a PNG file.' Then it is made of chunks, like building blocks, each with its own type and data. The first chunk has the image size and color mode, the middle chunks have the picture itself, and the last chunk says 'I am done.'

sections.title: Color Modes and Image Data
sections.content:
PNG supports five color types. Indexed color (type 3) uses a palette of up to 256 colors and works well for graphics and diagrams; each pixel is stored as an index into the palette. Grayscale (type 0) represents shades of gray and can use 1, 2, 4, 8, or 16 bits per pixel. Truecolor (type 2) stores separate red, green, and blue channels at 8 or 16 bits each, supporting millions or billions of colors. Both grayscale and truecolor can optionally include an alpha channel (types 4 and 6), where each pixel has a transparency value: 0 means fully transparent, the maximum value means fully opaque, and intermediate values create semi-transparent pixels. Unlike some formats, PNG stores alpha as 'non-premultiplied', meaning the color values are preserved even for transparent pixels.

Image data in the IDAT chunk is organized as scanlines, one row of pixels at a time, and is always stored left to right and top to bottom (though optional interlacing can split the data across seven passes for progressive display). Before compression, each scanline can be filtered with one of five algorithms—None, Sub, Up, Average, or Paeth—that prepare the data for better deflate compression without losing any information. A filter byte precedes each scanline to indicate which filter was used.
sections.plainLanguage: PNG can store pictures in different ways: with a small palette of colors, as shades of gray, or with millions of colors. It can also store how see-through each pixel is. Before squeezing the picture with compression, PNG runs a filter on each row to make it squeeze better.

sections.title: Lossless Compression and Deflate
sections.content:
PNG uses deflate/inflate compression with a 32-kilobyte sliding window, the same algorithm used by zip and gzip. This method is patent-free and widely implemented. The RFC specifies that PNG compression method 0 (the only one defined) must use deflate wrapped in the zlib format, which adds a checksum to verify the compressed stream decompressed correctly.

Deflate itself works in two stages: the data is first encoded with LZ77 (a technique that replaces repeated patterns with references), then the result is encoded with Huffman codes (shorter codes for more frequent symbols). The compressed image data can be split across multiple IDAT chunks however the encoder wishes; chunk boundaries have no semantic meaning and can fall anywhere in the deflate stream. For very large or very small images, this splitting allows encoders to work with a fixed memory budget.

The combination of filtering (which makes the data less random) and deflate compression achieves very good compression on typical images. PNG is fully lossless: every pixel value is preserved exactly, making it suitable for scientific data, graphics, and any application where pixel-perfect fidelity is required.
sections.plainLanguage: PNG squeezes the picture using a free method called deflate that finds repeated patterns in the data and uses shorter codes for common values. The compressed data can be split into pieces if needed, and nothing is thrown away—the picture comes out exactly the same when you unsqueeze it.

sections.title: Features and Status
sections.content:
PNG's key features include support for interlaced transmission (allowing progressive display as the file arrives over a network), gamma and chromaticity metadata (so images display correctly on different screens), straightforward detection of file corruption via CRCs, and optional text chunks for storing copyright notices, creation dates, and other metadata. The format is designed to be robust: unknown chunks are safely ignored, and chunk properties encoded in the type code itself allow decoders to handle extensions gracefully.

RFC 2083 defines PNG Version 1.0. The format is now Historic; later versions have been published, and new image formats have emerged for specialized purposes (such as HEIF for video-optimized compression and WebP for web delivery). However, PNG remains widely used and implemented wherever lossless compression and broad compatibility are required. The web, scientific applications, and many graphics tools still depend on PNG as a reliable, unencumbered standard for storing images.
sections.plainLanguage: PNG can store extra information in the picture file, like when it was made or who owns it. It handles mistakes well, so a corrupted file is usually easy to spot. Although PNG is old now, it is still used everywhere on the internet and in offices because it works well and anyone can use it for free.

data.title: PNG file signature and chunk structure

fields.name: PNG Signature Byte 1
fields.desc: Byte value 137 (0x89), a non-printable character to detect text-mode corruption.

fields.name: PNG Signature (ASCII)
fields.desc: ASCII letters 'PNG' (80, 78, 71), recognizable as the PNG format.

fields.name: PNG Signature Byte 4-8
fields.desc: Bytes 13, 10, 26, 10 (CRLF, EOF, LF), detecting line-ending and EOF corruption.

fields.name: Chunk Length
fields.desc: 4-byte unsigned integer: number of bytes in the chunk data, not including length, type, or CRC.

fields.name: Chunk Type Code
fields.desc: 4-byte ASCII code (e.g., IHDR, IDAT, IEND). Case of each letter encodes chunk properties.

fields.name: Chunk Data
fields.desc: Variable-length data specific to the chunk type (shown as 32 bits in example).

fields.name: Chunk CRC
fields.desc: 4-byte CRC calculated over chunk type and data; detects transmission errors.
